article_text:
Italian artist Marisa Merz (1926–2019) was famously camera-shy. In rare snapshots, such as a captivating photograph taken by Claudio Abate at her 1975 solo show in Rome, she would retreat from the camera’s gaze. Before Abate’s camera, Merz appears clad in her woven nylon Scarpette (Little Shoes) , 1968, her back to him as she gazes out an open window at the moon.

The turn away is emblematic of Merz’s artistic ethos writ large. As she once wrote, in a 1975 issue of Data Arte magazine, “The artist is already an established role, like the wife, the son. But I don’t go along with these roles.”

Merz was the only woman affiliated with Arte Povera , a loose movement christened in 1967 by curator Germano Celant that rejected the commodification of art and celebrated presence and materiality through nontraditional media and process-based practices. Even within this iconoclast milieu, she remained an outlier, not only for her inscription of domestic labor into her work—in her 1967 film The Count , she is seen in her kitchen sorting beans—but also for her use of figuration from the 1970s onward. Her unruly aluminum installations, paraffin pools, and woven forms were overlooked in the 1960s and 1970s, but she has gained wider recognition in recent years. Since the 1990s, major exhibitions of her work have been staged across Europe and the US, and in 2013, the Venice Biennale honored her with a Golden Lion.

Still, Merz remains evasive even as she enters the spotlight. A sprawling and polyphonic retrospective titled “Marisa Merz: La danza delle ore (The Dance of the Hours)” has taken over three Turin institutions on the centenary of her birth. Yet despite its exhaustive review of more than five decades of her work, she remains enigmatic. The Galleria d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea Torino (GAM) emphasizes her superposition of studio and home; the Fondazione Merz focuses on her material experiments; and the Castello di Rivoli explores her metaphysical engagement with space. All the while, Merz’s elusive central themes—transparency, metamorphosis, and alchemy—recur throughout.

True to the retrospective’s title, the suite of exhibitions doesn’t follow a chronological itinerary, if only because to do so is nearly impossible. Her biography remains shrouded in mystery. These are the known facts of her life before 1960: Born in Turin to a father employed by Fiat, she studied dance and later modeled in other artists’ studios. Even after garnering critical attention, she rarely titled or dated her compositions and struggled to lay them to rest. The title of her first and best-known installation, The Living Sculpture (1966), says it all, encoding her belief that completion is concomitant to a kind of death.

This unsettled attitude manifests in a provisional quality that prevails across the works on view. The Living Sculpture is a tentacular, sewn-aluminum work that originally dangled claustrophobically from the ceilings of her home and now hangs in glittering fragments at GAM and Castello di Rivoli. Her series of knobby clay “Testine (Little Heads),” made from the 1970s to the 2010s, are unfired and sometimes retain the rough corners with which they were cut in bricklike masses from a larger block of clay. Her abstracted faces, painted and drawn on paper, wood, and alabaster, are warped and blurred as if in motion; one untitled and undated graphite physiognomy rearranges itself in whirling lines of vortex-like eyes.

Merz, like her Arte Povera peers, was frustrated by fixity and drawn to materials that morph across time. Perhaps appropriately, the curators have displayed works that may be unfinished and come straight from the studio; whether she planned to continue them will never be known. Notes on hotel stationery and Post-its remain tacked, taped, and clipped directly onto her drawings and paintings, variably describing the emotions she hoped to capture (for example, “expressive and polished”), quoting from literature (one composition glosses Hölderlin’s final poem), or simply logging dimensions. There is a sense that Merz might yet return with needle, pencil, or brush and pick up where she left off.

As if to show how an idea remains unfixed, persisting and evolving as later generations take it on, the exhibitions stage encounters between Merz and contemporary women artists—including Leonor Antunes, Thea Djordjadze, and Miriam Cahn—whose work shares affinities with hers. Tacita Dean was commissioned to produce a body of film and photographs in Merz’s home and studio. The results include a 16 mm film diptych Via Milano 13 (2026) capturing scenes from Merz’s apartment near Turin’s Porta Palazzo market. In slow frames, we see a honeycombed assemblage of cardboard cylinders from rolls of toilet paper and paper towels; a chorus of “Testine” arranged on the spiraling table in her husband’s old studio; a painted, blue-haired visage with livid red lips fastened on a wall, its double mirrored upside-down in a glass surface below. Hung in constellated installations at GAM and Fondazione Merz, a complementary series of photographs likewise opens Merz’s private world to our curious eyes, often capturing works in situ among furniture and family photographs before their displacement to the exhibitions’ airy galleries. The film and images verge on invasion, contravening Merz’s injunction against photographic capture—except, of course, for the fact of the artist’s absence, palpable in Dean’s meditative, static shots.

Leaving this suite of exhibitions, I find Merz’s practice is even more fugitive than before. I am not the first critic to encounter this difficulty. Writing on her work for Artforum in 1992, Celant reflected, “The instant it is defined, it flees.” Like the artist herself, Merz’s works are chimerical, morphing with the shifting light, blurring at the edges of the frame, slipping out of sight.

Foto: Paulina Mellado.", "credit": "Artishock"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Periferia no como lugar, sino como posición"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Periferia” es una palabra que Martelli usa a propósito, porque así es como buena parte del mundo del arte ha aprendido a mirar a los espacios independientes: como aquello que está fuera, alrededor o frente a un centro que ya estaría establecido. Los demás orbitan como satélites."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "OtherNetwork se ha preguntado siempre qué ocurre si se invierte esa jerarquía, si, en lugar de acercar esos espacios al centro, cada uno pudiera pensarse como un centro en sí mismo. “Hoy, la manera en que la cultura se define, se discute y se escribe siempre viene del centro, y por centro no me refiero solo a los museos, aunque son una parte importante. Esos son los epicentros”, afirma Martelli."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "En un mundo digitalmente interconectado, una escena artística está hecha de muchas escenas simultáneas. article_text:
OtherNetwork es una red internacional que enlaza espacios artísticos independientes de geografías diversas para multiplicar los nodos desde los que la cultura puede producirse y movilizarse. Hablamos con su fundador, Federico Martelli, sobre cómo descentralizar los circuitos culturales y construir infraestructura y vínculos de largo plazo desde la pequeña escala.

Los espacios de arte independientes suelen funcionar con poco: equipos pequeños, presupuestos inciertos, muchas veces una mezcla de autogestión y apoyos puntuales. Pero esa precariedad no necesariamente se traduce en falta de libertad. Para Federico Martelli , fundador de OtherNetwork , los artistas encuentran en estos espacios más autonomía para trabajar, sobre todo en contextos de democracias frágiles o gobiernos autoritarios. Allí percibe otros modos de montar exposiciones y de trabajar con los artistas, menos sujetos a las reglas de las grandes instituciones.

La pandemia hizo más evidente la fragilidad de esos espacios. Los recortes presupuestarios que vinieron después terminaron de ponerla sobre la mesa. ¿Qué pasaría con ellos? ¿Cómo podían ayudarse entre sí? La idea de OtherNetwork comenzó a tomar forma a partir de esas preguntas.

El proyecto fue concebido originalmente por el estudio de diseño Cookies , con sede en Rotterdam, del que forma parte Federico Martelli, en colaboración con el Institut für Auslandsbeziehungen ( ifa ) de Alemania. Iniciado en 2021, buscaba conectar espacios independientes de diferentes partes del mundo y reunir los fondos que les permitieran colaborar entre sí. Hoy, OtherNetwork opera como una fundación sin fines de lucro registrada en los Países Bajos, con un equipo distribuido entre Europa, África y América Latina. Su trabajo se ha ido armando desde esos vínculos, como una red que parte de los espacios y las personas que la componen.

Periferia no como lugar, sino como posición

“Periferia” es una palabra que Martelli usa a propósito, porque así es como buena parte del mundo del arte ha aprendido a mirar a los espacios independientes: como aquello que está fuera, alrededor o frente a un centro que ya estaría establecido. Museos, galerías comerciales, grandes instituciones. Los demás orbitan como satélites.

OtherNetwork se ha preguntado siempre qué ocurre si se invierte esa jerarquía, si, en lugar de acercar esos espacios al centro, cada uno pudiera pensarse como un centro en sí mismo. “Hoy, la manera en que la cultura se define, se discute y se escribe siempre viene del centro, y por centro no me refiero solo a los museos, aunque son una parte importante. También me refiero a las revistas que se posicionan como referentes del gusto, a los lugares donde se escribe crítica y se decide qué es bueno y qué no. Esos son los epicentros”, afirma Martelli.

En un mundo digitalmente interconectado, una escena artística está hecha de muchas escenas simultáneas. La oposición entre centro y periferia puede dar paso a una estructura donde coexisten múltiples centros que se definen según los vínculos que se tejen entre ellos. La periferia, entonces, cuestiona la existencia del centro como única medida de legitimidad. “Todo se vuelve red, todo se vuelve nodo, y cada uno puede reclamar un pedacito del centro para sí. Así es como jugamos con la noción de periferia; en el fondo, es una propuesta”, dice Martelli.

¿Qué significa ser independiente?

Responder qué es un espacio independiente es más complejo de lo que parece. Lo que algunos entienden como autonomía, para otros puede significar algo completamente distinto. Martelli se encontró con esa dificultad al intentar ordenar los espacios que integran OtherNetwork. “En Kinshasa, la independencia tiene mucho más que ver con lo político: la libertad de no ser censurado. Es una forma profunda de independencia, una que quizás damos por sentada en un lugar como Rotterdam. Aunque incluso eso está cambiando: con la situación en Gaza e Israel, hay una presión real en la escena cultural para guardar silencio sobre el genocidio. No siempre es censura directa, pero se siente”.

En los Países Bajos, en cambio, hay espacios que se consideran independientes y que reciben una proporción considerable de su financiamiento del Estado. Las condiciones políticas y los modelos de financiamiento varían de un contexto a otro, y con ellos cambia también el significado de la palabra “independiente”.

La propia plataforma tuvo que enfrentarse a esa noción difusa. Cuando se trabaja con una red internacional, hay que encontrar categorías que permitan ordenar la información y la gestión, pero esas categorías no siempre alcanzan para describir lo que ocurre en la práctica. Por eso, una de las primeras series editoriales de OtherNetwork, Interdependence , invitó a diversos espacios a proponer autores que hablaran de sus propias ideas sobre la independencia.

El ejercicio no resolvió del todo la discusión y despertó otra pregunta: ¿independiente respecto de qué?

Para OtherNetwork, la independencia se entiende frente a aquello de lo que un espacio busca mantenerse autónomo: el Estado, el mercado, una institución o las estructuras de poder de una escena. Pero esa autonomía puede convivir con otros modos de dependencia. Justamente, esa falta de una definición única es la que permite que la conversación siga abierta.

Un mapa que produce conexiones

El mapa del sitio web de OtherNetwork ubica a los espacios en las ciudades y pueblos donde desarrollan su trabajo, sin agruparlos por países. “Creemos que es a escala de ciudad donde vivimos como humanos, de persona a persona, y ahí es donde estos espacios independientes son más activos y efectivos”. Para Martelli, importa dónde está cada lugar y también con quién se vincula. “El mapa no solo registra conexiones, también las produce y las fortalece”.

Una de las vías para lograrlo es el relay , un sistema de relevo en el que un espacio anfitrión invita al siguiente a realizar una exposición. Así, una cadena puede comenzar en Stuttgart, continuar en Accra y Johannesburgo, pasar luego por Brasil y Puerto Rico, llegar a Barranquilla y seguir hasta Guatemala.

El relay cuenta con el financiamiento de ifa y con el acompañamiento de OtherNetwork, que aporta apoyo en producción, comunicación y otros aspectos prácticos, pero no interviene en las decisiones curatoriales de los espacios, de modo que los nuevos vínculos surgen de los lazos que se forman entre quienes participan.

“Nos convertimos en una especie de institución fantasma, un museo descentralizado: financiamiento, material gráfico, apoyo profesional, comunicación; todo lo que hace un museo, pero sin el museo. Cada conexión genera la siguiente y, sobre todo, construye confianza”, explica Martelli.

Una red también precaria

Hay, sin embargo, una paradoja en el desarrollo de este sistema. La sostenibilidad de OtherNetwork es tan frágil como la de muchos de los espacios que busca enlazar. “Funcionamos un poco como una organización paraguas: intentamos ser profesionales, tenemos un equipo maravilloso, le dedicamos mucho de nuestro propio tiempo a que esto ocurra. Proyectamos la sensación de ser algo asentado y sólido, pero somos tan precarios como todos los demás”, afirma Martelli.

Esta constatación ha llevado a OtherNetwork a replantear su lugar dentro de la red. Si es también un proyecto independiente, tampoco queda a salvo de las dificultades que enfrentan sus miembros. En realidad, comparte muchos de sus problemas, como un participante más de una trama en la que todos tienen distintos grados de vulnerabilidad.

“Si nosotros también somos un proyecto de arte independiente, entonces somos pares dentro de la red, no un agente externo que ofrece ayuda”, explica.

Esto obliga a la organización a pensar cómo se distribuyen los recursos en un entorno donde las diferencias entre los miembros pueden ser enormes. Mientras algunas organizaciones cuentan con equipos y estructuras consolidadas, otras pueden estar funcionando al límite de su capacidad. OtherNetwork intenta tener esas diferencias en cuenta y poner más recursos donde hacen más falta. El objetivo es evitar que una red internacional reproduzca las mismas jerarquías que pretende cuestionar.

El primer evento local organizado por OtherNetwork como parte de su programa cultural internacional de 2023 se llevó a cabo en Espacio Odeón, en el que seis invitados hablaron sobre su experiencia en la creación, dirección o gestión de proyectos culturales independientes en la capital colombiana.

Pero no siempre es fácil. Las capacidades y modos de trabajo de cada espacio difieren, y al colaborar pueden surgir fricciones. Para OtherNetwork, esas fricciones son un aprendizaje inherente al trabajar entre personas y organizaciones que no se conocen, en contextos diferentes. De ahí surge Navigating Frictions , una serie de editoriales sobre cómo moverse entre esas diferencias e incorporarlas a la construcción de la red.

“Intentamos aprender de la fricción. La fricción es lo que nos mantiene vivos, es con lo que la mayoría de estas organizaciones ha tenido que aprender a lidiar. Nuestro rol es navegar esas dinámicas: ser un catalizador, o una especie de lubricante entre las partes, para asegurarnos de que las cosas realmente pasen”, señala Martelli.

Ese trabajo también exige atender a las dinámicas de poder que pueden reproducirse dentro de la propia red. Martelli explica que gran parte de las conversaciones internas del equipo gira en torno a cómo evitar actuar como gatekeepers y cómo impedir que lo que están tejiendo se convierta en un caso más de extractivismo cultural.

El relay también cumple una función en ese sentido, porque reparte la toma de decisiones entre quienes participan. La intención, dice, es que las partes vinculadas compartan agencia, que cada participante se sienta valorado y que los recursos y beneficios de la red se distribuyan de forma justa.

Sostener una red

Toda esta estructura necesita, por supuesto, recursos. ifa, institución alemana vinculada al Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores, es desde el inicio el principal socio de OtherNetwork. Aportó el financiamiento inicial y hoy financia íntegramente el relay de exposiciones, la actividad más costosa de la red, que ambas organizaciones desarrollan en conjunto.

Para ifa, el proyecto fue en parte un experimento. Su Departamento de Artes Visuales lleva más de cuarenta años desarrollando exposiciones itinerantes, que tradicionalmente trasladaban obras producidas en un lugar hacia otros destinos, con poca participación local. Junto a OtherNetwork, la institución se abrió a probar un modelo distinto, que sigue vigente: poner en conversación a espacios independientes y dejar que los proyectos se hagan desde sus propios contextos.

Con el tiempo, OtherNetwork se constituyó como fundación en los Países Bajos. Por razones administrativas, esa figura le permite acceder a otras fuentes de financiamiento, sin cambiar el vínculo con ifa, que sigue siendo su socio principal. La organización también ha recibido apoyo de instituciones como Stimuleringsfonds y Between Bridges , la fundación que creó el reconocido fotógrafo Wolfgang Tillmans. Diversificar las fuentes de financiamiento sigue siendo un desafío, y es parte de la conversación sobre qué significa ser independiente.

“Más allá de ser un proyecto cultural que postula a fondos culturales, esperamos acceder a una filantropía con un enfoque más social, orientada a fortalecer la sociedad. No ha sido fácil: son círculos difíciles de entrar y estamos siguiendo activamente algunas pistas. Además, nos estamos abriendo a donaciones individuales”, detalla Martelli.

Del mapa digital al encuentro físico

Una de las cosas que OtherNetwork descubrió en el camino fue que la relación entre lo digital y lo presencial terminó siendo distinta de lo que habían imaginado. Al comienzo, Martelli pensaba que la página web sería el centro del proyecto y que los encuentros físicos funcionarían como una extensión. Ocurrió exactamente al revés.

“Lo más importante terminaron siendo los eventos, las cosas que se hacen en la vida real, y son esas cosas reales las que construyen la plataforma digital”, cuenta. Pero el sitio web se fortalece en paralelo. Es un archivo en constante crecimiento. “Partió muy esquelético, pero hoy puedes rastrear cosas que pasaron hace tres años o más. Esperamos que sea útil para creadores, curadores y para cualquiera que estudie cómo ocurre realmente la cultura”.

OtherNetwork entiende ahora que su verdadera función es generar las condiciones para que los espacios se vinculen y, más importante aún, para que esos nexos continúen en el tiempo. Bocas de agua , la sexta exposición del relay, es un buen ejemplo. Esta vez, Casa de Meira , en Barranquilla, invitó a La Nueva Fábrica , de Antigua Guatemala, a desarrollar una propuesta en la ciudad. La exposición se presenta del 15 de octubre al 12 de noviembre en la Galería de Bellas Artes de la Universidad del Atlántico y reúne a artistas de Colombia, Guatemala, Puerto Rico, Costa Rica, Brasil, Trinidad y Tobago y Chile.

Ilaria Conti , directora y curadora de La Nueva Fábrica, toma como punto de partida Barranquilla y su diálogo con el río Magdalena y el Caribe para organizar esta exposición en torno al agua, la interdependencia y los vínculos entre cuerpos, territorios y saberes.

Trabajar desde la pequeña escala

En medio de crisis políticas, sociales y ecológicas en distintas partes del mundo, Martelli reivindica la importancia del arte y la cultura como espacios de diálogo. Pero, en el caso de OtherNetwork, no imagina responder a estas circunstancias con una organización cada vez más grande que busque cubrir más frentes.

“El sueño es convertirnos en una herramienta más abierta, diversa y accesible. En estos años hemos construido una especie de familia a través de estos eventos y exposiciones. Nos encantaría mantener vivas esas relaciones con más oportunidades a pequeña escala, no megaproyectos. La pequeña escala es donde queremos trabajar”.

El impacto de una plataforma como esta se mide en años. Los fondos llegan y se acaban, las exposiciones y eventos tienen fecha de cierre, pero la confianza entre dos espacios de arte que se conocieron a través de un relevo puede perdurar. Lo que propone OtherNetwork es una apuesta: que las iniciativas pequeñas, con paciencia, dejen huella.

article_text:
Oscar-nominated composer Daniel Pemberton is a quadruple threat — at least — this year with scores in four movies, as well as the TV series “Slow Horses.”

The British film music writer composed the soundtracks to movies including “The Drama,” with its mischievous flutes recorded at Abbey Road Studios; “Masters of the Universe”; and Oscar contenders “Ink,” “ Project Hail Mary ,” and “Musk.” On this week’s edition of IndieWire’s “ Screen Talk ” podcast, co-hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio spoke to Pemberton about his multi-hyphenate journey to composing, which began in video games but included breakout work on Ridley Scott’s “The Counselor.”

“With ‘Hail Mary,’ it was like it had no map, and it was like we gotta make this up as we go along. And that’s thrilling, but also terrifying. And so we spent a huge amount of time, like, just trying out ideas, experimenting, finding unusual textures and sounds, approaches, and that would slowly feed itself into the movie or end up in the bin,” said Pemberton, who also wrote an original song called “Let Me Sell You a Dream” that’s sung by David Byrne in Alex Gibney’s “Musk.” ( Gibney was the special guest on last week’s episode of “Screen Talk.” )

Elsewhere on the podcast, we also review (i.e., eviscerate) Taika Waititi’s confoundingly awful dystopian sci-fi movie “ Klara and the Sun ,” an adaptation of Nobel Prize-winning author Kazuo Ishiguro and starring Jenna Ortega, who’s on a big-screen losing streak after terrible reviews for her last several movies. Like her co-star Amy Adams, she’s faring better these days on television (see Netflix’s “Wednesday”).

We also catch up on “I Play Rocky” and the latest developments in the awards season race — plus, the C-suite freefall happening at Netflix amid the ousting of film head Dan Lin.

article_text:
“ You Can See Everything ,” an intimate look at Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has earned nearly $80 million at the domestic box office , becoming A24 ‘s third-highest-grossing release in North America. It bypasses “Everything Everywhere All at Once” and its $77 million haul to take its spot on the indie studio’s chart, and that film won the Oscar for Best Picture.

With $79.8 million stateside, “You Can See Everything” sits behind the summer blockbuster “Backrooms” ($197 million) and 2025’s “Marty Supreme” ($96 million) on the list of A24 releases. Other A24 films made more globally, with “Backrooms” earning more than $400 million, “Marty Supreme” grossing $192.4 million, and “Everything Everywhere All at Once” netting $147.9 million.

However, “You Can See Everything” has yet to be released in most international markets. It’s unclear if Holmes’ fraud will resonate with moviegoers so far from Silicon Valley. It doesn’t matter if it doesn’t connect, because with a budget of $7 million, “You Can See Everything” is already wildly profitable. Its success means that Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the directing duo behind the doc, are now in high demand.

“You Can See Everything” also jumped ahead of “March of the Penguins” ($77 million) on the list of highest-grossing documentaries in North America. Variety reports that makes it the second highest-grossing doc behind Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which earned $119 million domestically. That doesn’t account for music documentaries like “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour” ($267.1 million) and “Michael Jackson’s This is It” ($268 million), which were far more popular.

A24 is on a hot streak . In addition to “Backrooms,” the indie studio has released hits like “The Drama” and “Primetime.” Its latest film, “ Club Kid ,” grossed an impressive $390,583 this weekend when it opened on six screens in New York and Los Angeles. That’s a per-screen average of $65,097. A24 acquired the drama about a hard-living gay man and his son out of the Cannes Film Festival, where it debuted to raves. The studio hopes to position the film and its writer, director, and star Jordan Firstman in the Oscar race.

article_text:
Films and events

First Feature Competition

Lady

In a bustling Lagos, a solitary female taxi driver finds community among a group of sex workers as she transports them around the city.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Olive Nwosu

With Jessica Gabriel’s Ujah, Amanda Oruh, Tinuade Jemiseye

UK-Nigeria 2026. 93min

Courtesy of Metis Films

Language Nigerian Pidgin With English subtitles

Access information

Saturday 10 October 21:00

Audio description

Tuesday 13 October 12:10

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Lady works long and lonely hours, saving up money with hopes of escaping to Freetown, in Sierra Leone. When childhood friend and sex worker Pinky asks for her help, Lady agrees but soon finds her life upended. The fantastic, mainly female cast shared the Sundance Film Festival Special Jury Award for Acting Ensemble. It’s easy to see why, with this character-driven film that is also a stunning portrait of a vibrant, sleepless city.

Grace Barber-Plentie

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury, nudity, and sex.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Clarissa

Sophie Okonedo shines in Arie and Chuko Esiri’s (Eyimofe, LFF 2020) sophomore feature film, a delicate, sun-soaked re-imagining of Mrs Dalloway, set in contemporary Lagos.

Filipiñana

This bold debut, set over the course of one sweltering day, follows a 17-year-old working as a ‘tee-girl’ at a golf club.

Our Share of Sand

Shalini Adnani’s poignant coming-of-age drama presents a unique perspective on India’s gaping class inequality, child labour and the deep corruption underpinning a family’s economic status.

Editor’s note: T his story contains details of alleged sexual offenses that some readers may find distressing .

Russell Brand was told he “has a platform with followers in the millions” and has not been “taken apart by the media” during questioning by the prosecution today at Southwark Crown Court.

Brand was being probed by barrister Riel Karmy-Jones over his attacks on the press after allegations were made in a Channel 4 documentary and in The Times in 2023, which led six women to go to the police with similar allegations about him.

Brand has repeatedly criticized large portions of the media for the way in which he has been portrayed since 2023 and uses his Rumble social media platform to communicate his message.

Watch on Deadline

While Brand earlier told the court “no one will touch me with a bargepole” since the documentary, Karmy-Jones said it is “not the case you have been completely abandoned by everyone,” as she pointed out he was playing a show to a packed house of around 2,000 people in London when the doc came out.

“You have a platform with followers in the millions, don’t you?” she told the court. “This is not a case of ‘Poor Mr Brand’ who’s been taken apart by the media and the social construct.”

At this point in proceedings, the judge told Karmy-Jones to move on with her questioning.

Just before that, when it was put to him that the media had been “very fair” to him by allowing him to respond in detail to the documentary’s allegations before it aired, Brand said he “would reject that quite strongly.”

He vociferously responded “Yes” to the question of whether he “blames” Channel 4’s Dispatches show and the media more broadly for the situation he currently finds himself in.

Brand was told by Karmy-Jones he had been “liberally speaking” about portions of the media and these allegations on his own platform since being charged, but he responded by saying he “has done my very best to respect this judicial process and the integrity of this court.”

Brand was cross-examined by the prosecution after facing questions from his defense lawyer Ian Winter , during which he forcefully denied the charges and said his “entire life has been consumed by these allegations.” Brand faces three charges of rape, three counts of sexual assault and now one of attempted indecent assault, reduced from indecent assault, based on allegations made by six women . Deadline has been reporting daily from a live video feed of the courtroom since the trial began.

Pressed on why it is only recently, and after his police interviews, that he has started recalling details of the three rape allegations, Brand said it has “taken a lot of focus and recollection to do the best I can to participate in this.”

Regarding Complainant 1, who alleges Brand raped her in a hotel room at the fringes of the Labour Party conference in 1999, he rejected the idea that he “stood in between her and the exit” and “pushed her on the bed against her will.”

Instead, he recalled he “asked for more than [C1’s] consent.”

Regarding Complainant 3, who alleges Brand orally raped her in a toilet cubicle at a birthday party, Brand denied “pulling her head down violently onto your penis” as it was put to him by Karmy-Jones.

“You liked ejaculating without a condom, and you ejaculated into her mouth,” questioned Karmy-Jones. “You said, ‘Don’t be a spoilsport, come on?’”

Brand replied “no” loudly to these questions. He acknowledged it was “within the bounds of possibility” that a rapist could hold someone’s head down and perform forced oral sex in such a way.

On Complainant 5, who alleges Brand anally raped her at his flat after they’d had consensual vaginal sex, Brand denied the allegation and said he “did not view [C5] as just a hole,” as C5 had claimed.

He said he could not remember C5 leaving blood and feces on his sheets, as she has alleged. He said “recollections increased” of C5 after he watched police interviews of her accusations and remembered she was the “memorable young woman” who had put her tongue in his anus after a play he performed. This was a few days before the alleged anal rape took place.

Goal To Sleep With 5,000 Women

Karmy-Jones repeatedly brought up Brand’s promiscuity during the era the allegations were alleged to have taken place.

He was questioned about a conversation in the car he had with his old flatmate on the way to the Labour conference in 1999, when he was accused of saying he had a goal to sleep with 5,000 women. “While I don’t remember, it’s entirely possible it’s the kind of banter I would have engaged in when I was 24,” he said.

He was accused of “doing anything” to get women into bed with him but retorted that “the way this has been characterized is so nefarious, unpleasant and ugly that it is difficult to answer in earnest.”

Asked if he had said he would not leave a situation with a woman without a conquest, he said: “That sounds specifically like a riff on a Woody Allen joke when he said the only advice my dad ever gave me on his death bed was ‘always try and f*** the waitress’.”

The trial continues.

Spain’s Valladolid International Film Festival – known in Spain as Seminci – opens Friday, Oct. 23 with 30 world premieres and a lineup bringing together some of international cinema’s most acclaimed auteurs and an emerging generation of Spanish filmmakers.

Running through Oct. 31, the festival’s 71st edition features 22 films in official competition and 208 titles overall — 137 features and 71 shorts — including 121 premieres.

The gathering is being steered by two longtime members of the team that helped shape Seminci’s recent artistic identity. Mariona Viader, previously general coordinator, and Javier H. Estrada, formerly head of programming, have stepped in as interim co-directors following the death of dynamic festival director José Luis Cienfuegos in December, maintaining the programming vision he introduced in 2023.

Popular on Variety

The selection embraces widely different approaches to filmmaking, from formally experimental work to more accessible independent productions, while exploring political upheaval, memory, exile and intimate family relationships.

“What matters about Seminci is that our programming allows us to explore what auteur cinema means,” Estrada says.

Acclaimed Voices, New Perspectives

Among the contenders for Valladolid’s top prize, the Golden Spike, are May el-Toukhy’s “Woman Unknown,” winner of Venice’s Golden Lion, and İlker Çatak’s Berlin Golden Bear winner “Yellow Letters.”

“When we selected the films for Seminci, we had no idea ‘Woman Unknown’ would win the Golden Lion,” Estrada says.

Elsewhere in the competition, Alain Gomis’ “Dao” connects a wedding in France with a memorial ceremony in Guinea-Bissau, weaving family histories across continents. In “Double Freedom,” Lisandro Alonso returns to the world of his breakthrough “La libertad” 25 years later, revisiting ideas of solitude and independence.

In Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose,” Berlin best performance winner Sandra Hüller plays a woman passing herself off as a man in 17th-century Europe. Lance Hammer’s “Queen at Sea,” starring Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay, turns to the complexities of family relationships.

Bernardo Bertolucci’s final co-written screenplay provides the basis for Andrea Pallaoro’s “The Echo Chamber,” starring Alicia Vikander and Susan Sarandon.

The festival’s opening and closing films reinforce its mix of distinctive filmmaking voices and international star power. Hungarian director Lili Horvát , who won Valladolid’s Golden Spike in 2020, returns with “My Notes on Mars,” starring Mackenzie Davis (“Blade Runner 2049”). Gael García Bernal closes the event with “Hombre al agua,” his third directorial feature.

The Significance of a World Premiere

While many of the international competition titles have already made their mark on the festival circuit, 30 films — just over half of them Spanish productions or co-productions — will face their first audiences at Seminci.

“A world premiere always entails a certain vulnerability for filmmakers,” Estrada says. “The fact that so many films choose Seminci for their world premieres is a great responsibility. We have to take care of each film. But it’s also a cause for celebration. The moment audiences see a film for the first time is truly exciting.”

The Spanish selection includes established genre directors alongside filmmakers making their feature debuts.

Daniel Calparsoro’s “El confidente,” screening in the official selection out of competition, is set during the final years of Basque terrorist group ETA and stars Javier Gutiérrez and Miguel Herrán. Bowfinger International Pictures produces.

Also screening out of competition is David Martín de los Santos’ Spanish-Peruvian co-production “Un hombre en un puente,” involving Vértigo Films.

Family relationships emerge as a recurring theme across the Spanish selection, particularly among filmmakers exploring the bonds, conflicts and shifting definitions of family.

“Rethinking the concept of family is one of the central themes of this year’s Seminci,” Estrada says.

Actor Ricardo Gómez’s directing debut “Una familia,” screening out of competition and distributed in Spain by Filmax, explores the secrets and unresolved wounds shaping relationships between parents and children. Meanwhile, Ione Hernández Sáenz’s feature debut “Hermanas,” starring Elena Anaya and Emma Suárez, competes for the Golden Spike with a drama about two sisters whose relationship is tested by a family crisis.

The theme also extends to the Meeting Point competition, where Sandra Sánchez’s “A nadadora” follows a teenager struggling with a troubled family background, while Ledicia Sola’s “As augas” explores the possibility of redefining family through friendship. Both have their world premieres in Valladolid, alongside Marc Ferrer’s black-and-white satirical comedy “Cinemanía,” which previously participated in ECAM Forum’s Last Push.

Another discovery is Claudia Estrada Tarascó’s feature debut “Salen las lobas,” inspired by her sister’s experiences in a juvenile justice facility. For Oceanika’s producer Alba Sotorra, its Valladolid launch comes at a key moment for the film.

“Seminci is a strategic place to present Claudia Estrada’s first film, both because of its international reach and its standing in Spain,” Sotorra says.

Beyond the debut features, Spanish cinema is also represented in the Golden Spike competition by animation and independent co-productions.

Ervin Han and Raúl García’s “The Violinist,” a Singapore-led co-production from Robot Playground Media, Spain’s TV ON Producciones and Italy’s Altri Occhi, won Annecy’s best feature Cristal and SACEM music prize ahead of its Nov. 13 Spanish theatrical release via Wanda Visión.

Helena Girón and Samuel Delgado’s “Las islas afortunadas” competes for the Golden Spike following its Toronto world premiere. Bendita Film Sales handles international sales of this period drama, whose producers are in talks with several distributors for a potential Spanish theatrical release.

A festival selection may not seal a deal, but it can “give negotiations the push they sometimes need,” says Bendita CEO Luis Renart.

The world premieres also extend beyond feature films. Movistar Plus unveils the first three episodes of crime thriller “Killing a Bear” (Matar a un oso”), created by Jorge and Alberto Sánchez-Cabezudo, starring Eduard Fernández and co-produced with Arte France.

Meanwhile, “SerYo,” an El Terrat documentary co-directed by Sergio Peris-Mencheta, Marta Solaz and Verónica Díaz Pérez, explores artistic creation during Peris-Mencheta’s illness.

Five Iranian filmmakers feature across Seminci’s lineup, including Ali Asgari’s “A Bit of Light,” Pegah Ahangarani’s documentary “Essays for a Revolution” and films by Mani Haghighi, Mahsa Karampour and Karim Lakzadeh. The independently selected works explore war, repression, exile and cultural identity.

“It was the quality of the films themselves, and above all how different they are from one another,” Estrada says. “Each filmmaker, in their own style, demonstrates the creative strength of Iranian cinema.”

Seminci’s appetite for adventurous filmmaking finds a particularly strong expression in Alchemies, a 10-film competition launched in 2023 and devoted to works that challenge conventional storytelling.

Highlights include Portuguese filmmakers João Pedro Rodrigues and João Rui Guerra da Mata’s “13 Pins,” blending religious imagery and desire; Ted Fendt’s Berlin-set “Foreign Travel”; and Karim Lakzadeh’s darkly comic “Living Twice, Dying Thrice,” about miners who fake their deaths to secure compensation for their families. Spanish contenders include David Baute’s “Benigno,” an intimate portrait of an elderly man living in his childhood home, and Sebastián Uría’s “Adiós, ríos,” exploring the disappearance of a rural community.

The non-competitive Memory & Utopia section revisits seven decades of cinema through 14 films exploring the interplay of fantasy, surrealism and historical memory. Highlights include the world premiere of the restored version of Ana Mariscal’s 1962 Franco-era spy thriller “Occidente y sabotaje,” 4K restorations of Luis Buñuel’s masterpice “Un chien andalou” and “L’Age d’Or,” and Yoshiaki Kawajiri’s anime landmark “Ninja Scroll.” The selection also features works by Věra Chytilová, Andrzej Wajda and Ildikó Enyedi.

Sound Moves to the Foreground

Seminci also devotes a major retrospective to the role of sound in cinema.

“The narrative power of sound often takes a back seat, and this year we wanted to bring it to the forefront,” Viader says.

The program moves from Fritz Lang’s “M” and Jacques Tati’s “Playtime” to Jonathan Glazer’s “The Zone of Interest,” exploring how filmmakers have used sound to convey information, build suspense and transform audiences’ emotional experiences.

An exhibition, publication and professional encounters developed with the European Film Academy’s Sound Chapter accompany the screenings.

Beyond its film program, Seminci also hosts the sixth Merci independent film market and the La Meseta labs, supporting independent theatrical distribution and short-film development.

The festival’s honorary awards recognize Valladolid-born Goya-winning actress Elvira Mínguez (“Tapas,” “Everybody Knows”) and Chilean filmmaker Valeria Sarmiento, presenting “Behind the Rain,” announced as her final film. The documentary filmmaking master’s program at Barcelona’s Pompeu Fabra University receives an Academic Honorary Golden Spike.

In keeping with the festival’s focus on sound, veteran Hollywood production sound mixer Willie D. Burton, an eight-time Oscar nominee and twice a winner, for “Bird” and “Dreamgirls,” receives an Honorary Golden Spike.

article_text:
The Indian actor Nana Patekar, who has died of a heart attack aged 75, first broke through in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay! (1988), and the Bollywood hits Parinda (1989) and Krantiveer (1994). These early credits established Patekar as a performer of rare versatility: he and Irrfan Khan remain the only performers to have won Filmfare’s best actor, best supporting actor and best villain awards (considered India’s “oscars”). Yet the question of whether Patekar was better suited to heroism or villainy lingered unresolved: allegations of sexual harassment and intimidation first made by his former co-star Tanushree Dutta in 2008 kickstarted India’s #MeToo movement when she raised them again in 2018.

Until that point, Patekar’s rougher edges had mostly been celebrated. As an actor, he demonstrated a baggy-eyed naturalism that spoke more to Bombay streetlife than Bollywood fantasy. He was given to writing out his dialogue until he had internalised it, and his growling line readings were both idiosyncratic and much imitated. Satyajit Ray counted among the actor’s most illustrious admirers, but apparently could not find a suitable project for him ; Patekar instead had Nair to thank for launching him to international prominence in Salaam Bombay! as Baba Golub, the brutal pimp and drug dealer lording over an army of street children.

Yet the Bollywood studios also made good use of his grouchy grit. He was commanding as the kingpin Anna in Parinda, Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s inventive relocation of On the Waterfront, for which Patekar won two best supporting actor awards; he was appointed an honorary captain in the Indian territorial army after undergoing three years of army training for Prahaar: The Final Attack (1991), a film he also ended up directing. He crossed paths with the emergent megastar Shah Rukh Khan in Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (1992) and was momentarily in the running for Subhash Ghai’s blockbuster Khalnayak (1993), losing out to Sanjay Dutt.

Relations between Patekar and Dutt deteriorated further after the latter was linked to the 1993 Bombay bus bombings in which Patekar’s brother was killed. (Patekar’s wife, the Marathi actor Neelakanti, was also due to board one of the targeted vehicles.) Even after Dutt’s comeback, Patekar remained defiant: “I have not worked with [Dutt] in 22 years of my career. I will not work with him in the future.”

A comparable rage powered Krantiveer, in which Patekar played a dissolute gambler reviving his fortunes via social activism. Heart problems meant he shot his final scenes with a doctor on standby; while distributors thought Patekar a commercial risk, the film struck a chord, becoming one of that year’s biggest Hindi hits.

Born Vishwanath Patekar in Murud-Janjira, Maharashtra, Nana was one of the three sons of Dinkar Patekar, a textile painter and businessman, and his wife, Nirmala. He was educated at the Samarth Vidyalaya and the Bandra School of Arts in Bombay (now Mumbai), supporting his family after his father’s business collapsed by painting zebra crossings and cinema posters. He went on to the Sir JJ Institute of Applied Art, where he also joined the drama society.

After graduation, he briefly worked as a police sketch artist before joining the Marathi theatre group Rangayan. Switched on to films by his friend the celebrated Indian actor Smita Patil (“I was happy doing theatre, but she insisted”), he made his screen debut in the 1978 social drama Gaman, starring Patil.

A string of supporting roles followed: two years before Salaam Bombay!, he played Gandhi’s assassin Nathuram Godse in the Emmy-winning TV miniseries Lord Mountbatten: The Last Viceroy.

Despite his success in Krantiveer, for which he won several best actor awards, Patekar was not always the easiest fit with the studio system. He was replaced on Raja (1995) after spending two days hectoring his co-stars Madhuri Dixit and Mukesh Khanna with acting notes. And he paused his career during the Kargil war of 1999 to enlist with the Maratha Light infantry, serving 60 days and earning a promotion to the rank of major.

Back on civvy street, he landed a signature role as Inspector Sadhu, the dirty cop who becomes the hero of Ab Tak Chhappan (2004), and swept India’s best villain prizes as the underworld don Tabrez Alam in Apaharan (2005). He then switched into a lighter mode for the knockabout comedies Welcome (2007) and Welcome Back (2015).

Elder statesman status beckoned: he played Mumbai’s police commissioner in The Attacks of 26/11 (2013), voiced Shere Khan in the Hindi dub of Disney’s The Jungle Book (2016) and enjoyed a major success with the Marathi film Natsamrat (2016), playing an acclaimed actor unravelling in retirement. He was awarded the Padma Shri and the Raj Kapoor special contribution award in 2013; in 2015, he set up the Naam Foundation with fellow actor Makarand Anaspure to help drought-hit farmers.

Then came Dutta’s 2018 interview with the Hindu , where she repeated an earlier accusation that Patekar had first sexually harassed her while shooting a dance sequence for Horn “OK” Pleassss (2009), then, when she fled the set, sent hired thugs after her. Footage of the incident aired on Indian TV showed a mob surrounding her car, her windscreen smashed and tyres being flattened. Patekar denied the allegations. The Mumbai police opened an investigation; while no formal charges were brought, the incident sparked renewed concern about the treatment of women in Bollywood.

After a spell in industry purdah, Patekar recently attempted a comeback. There were supporting turns in the propagandistic The Vaccine War (2023), limp comedy Housefull 5 (2025) and the streaming-bound Subedaar (2026), though the actor did lend a wry centre to Vishal Bhardwaj’s Shakespeare riff O’Romeo (2026).

He married Neelakanti in 1978, and they had two sons, the first of whom, Durvasa, died in 1980, aged two. Patekar is survived by his wife and his second son, Malhar.

article_text:
A major Paris art institution will host a significant Los Angeles collection next year. “ The Broad in Paris” (April 21–August 30, 2027), at the Fondation Louis Vuitton , will be the largest display of works from the Broad collection ever mounted outside its home city, with some 164 works making the transatlantic voyage. The show will happen while the Broad is closed for renovation; it will reopen in 2028 with 70 percent more gallery space.

“The Broad in Paris” will feature a star-studded roster of international contemporary figures such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Mark Bradford, Chris Burden, Sayre Gomez, Lauren Halsey, Keith Haring, William Kentridge, Barbara Kruger, Yayoi Kusama, Sherrie Levine, Roy Lichtenstein, Glenn Ligon, Julie Mehretu, Takashi Murakami, Laura Owens, Ed Ruscha, Cindy Sherman, Kara Walker, and Andy Warhol.

Opened in 2015 and founded by billionaire Eli Broad and his wife Edythe, the Broad collection is housed in a distinctive building by Diller Scofidio and Renfro, the first architecture firm to win a MacArthur Fellowship. Vuitton opened the year before in an equally notable structure by Frank Gehry, the 1989 winner of the Pritzker Prize, architecture’s highest honor.

The Broad exhibition follows other shows devoted to major institutions and collectors, such as “Icons of Modern Art: Shchukin” (2016–17), “Being Modern: MoMA in Paris” (2017), and “The Courtauld Collection: A Vision for Impressionism” (2019).

“We are two quite young institutions, both over a decade old, and we share a common purpose to present a deeper understanding of 20th- and 21st-century art,” said Broad founding director and president Joanne Heyeler in press materials. For her part, Suzanne Pagé, the Fondation Louis Vuitton’s artistic director, praised the Broad’s “clear and committed choices,” saying this show not only builds upon her institution’s past shows of artists such as Basquiat and Warhol but also offers “an opportunity to discover new artists from the Californian art scene.”

Heyeler and Pagé curated the show along with Broad curator and publications manager Ed Schad and Vuitton chief curator Olivier Michelon. A publication will illustrate every work in the show and include new commentary and essays.

article_text:
“The Batman: Part II” will soon resume production with Steven Soderbergh stepping in to finish principal photography while director Matt Reeves continues to attend to a family matter, IndieWire has confirmed.

Production on the Batman sequel at DC starring Robert Pattinson has been delayed for a little over a week as a result of Reeves’ absence.

“As Matt Reeves continues to attend to an ongoing family matter, Steven Soderbergh, as an admirer of Matt’s work, approached Matt and will step in to help the writer-director complete the final weeks of principal photography on ‘The Batman Part 2.’ Matt and Steven will work closely together with the actors and crew to fulfill Matt’s vision of the film ,” the studio said in a statement to IndieWire.

Soderbergh himself also added a statement: “I thought Matt Reeves’ work on ‘The Batman’ was stunning; it was intentional, specific, and rigorously coherent. The goal here is to work with Matt and his team to generate footage that will integrate seamlessly with what’s already been shot so Matt can properly finish his film.”

“The Batman: Part II” is dated for release on February 18, 2028 , and that date as of yet has not shifted amid the delay. There will be a six-year gap between the original “The Batman” with Pattinson and the sequel after the original grossed $772 million worldwide.

The new film sees Pattinson reprise his role as Bruce Wayne, alongside Colin Farrell returning as The Penguin and Andy Serkis returning as Alfred, and newcomers Sebastian Stan, Scarlett Johansson, Brian Tyree Henry, Jayme Lawson, Charles Dance, Gil Perez-Abraham, and Sebastian Koch. There’s rumors that Stan is playing Harvey Dent, a.k.a. Two Face, but that’s unclear. The only thing he had to say about the film to our Anne Thompson is that the film is “in a very deep, deep winter.”

Soderbergh is a fascinating name to work in a fill-in capacity, let alone on a tentpole superhero film. He obviously has history with Warner Bros. on the Ocean’s movies and with HBO and HBO Max on films like “No Sudden Move.” He is one of the quickest, most prolific directors working today , but this would represent his biggest film in a while and his only studio film since 2023’s “Magic Mike’s Last Dance.” And though he’s long been based in New York, he’s now based in London where “The Batman: Part II” is shooting.

His last narrative film was this year’s “The Christophers” from Neon, and he also directed a documentary, “John Lennon: The Last Interview,” that premiered at Cannes but is currently without distribution.
